raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented to our institution for evaluation of several multifocal chronic granulomatous skin lesions. He had a childhood history of asthma and pneumonia, as well as recurrent sinus infections requiring sinus surgery as an adult. Family history revealed a male cousin who was recently hospitalized for a disseminated Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection involving his liver. The patient denied any recent travel outside the country.
The skin lesions originally erupted seven years prior, starting as a non-painful, non-pruritic plaque on the right shoulder that remained persistent and eventually spread to all four extremities. Sarcoidosis was diagnosed at initial presentation and treated with corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine. Despite treatment and the initial response, skin lesions remained persistent, and thus subsequent skin biopsies were performed. Results yielded numerous acid-fast bacilli with granulomas. A tentative diagnosis of leprosy was given, and treatment with rifampin, clarithromycin, and minocycline ensued. Unfortunately, this regimen failed to yield any significant degree of improvement. Moreover, taper from the steroid treatment initially given for sarcoidosis was attempted, only to produce worsening of the skin lesions and development of high-grade fevers up to 105.0   F requiring hospitalization.
Due to pancytopenia, persistent fevers, and concern for disseminated infection or malignancy, a bone marrow biopsy was performed. Analysis of the biopsy demonstrated granulomas and acid-fast bacilli; culture isolates yielded Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI), rather than the preconceived Mycobacterium leprae. Based on these findings, antimicrobial therapy was changed to clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampin. Corticosteroids at a dose of 16 mg daily were also continued to prevent rebound exacerbation of the skin lesions.
Despite antibiotic therapy for six months, fevers persisted, and skin lesions advanced with new nodular masses developing quickly over the period of a week. Multiple ulcerations with overlying eschars on the right forearm and torso persisted, and large erythematous nodules with central low-grade ulceration formed on the right lower extremity. In addition, enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes concerning for granulomatous disease were visualized on CT scan.
A repeat skin biopsy showed a persistent MAI infection resistant to clarithromycin, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin. Additionally, the pathology report described an atypical T-cell infiltrate in the dermis and positive TCR gene rearrangement raising concern for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). At this time, the patient was referred to us for work-up of his potentially malignant skin condition. At presentation to our institution, lesions consisted of 3 to 4 inches in diameter, diffuse, raised, well-circumscribed erythematous red scaly plaques with a lack of active ulceration (Figure 1). Because of the concern for CTCL, further skin biopsies were performed. Results showed a histiocytic infiltrate admixed with very few small atypical lymphocytes (Figure 2) and long beaded bacilli consistent with mycobacterium, located in the superficial and deep dermis (Figure 3). Isolates demonstrated not only MAI, but also the presence of Mycobacterium simiae. Bone marrow core biopsy revealed a normocellular bone marrow constituents being populated by foamy histiocytes that are disposed in loosely formed granulomas (Figure 4). The admixed T-cells were clonal and appeared to lack CD7 by flow cytometry, but were positive for CD3, CD4, and CD26. However, the absence of epidermotropism, lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with acid-fast mycobacteria, and ultimately the marked paucity of T-cells and lymphocytes, rendered a clonal lymphoproliferative disorder involving the skin exceedingly unlikely. With CTCL effectively ruled out and compelling evidence of disseminated MAI infection, investigation into an underlying immune defect was performed. Evaluation of acquired immunodeficiencies associated with MAI infections was done, with negative antibodies to HIV and HTLV 1 and 2, and so a search for a primary immunodeficiency with susceptibility to non-tuberculous mycobacteria ensued. Based on family history implying X-linked inheritance, NEMO deficiency seemed most likely. A single base change of the last base of exon 1b (c.1-16G>C) of IKKg resulting in abnormally spliced transcripts and reduced expression of NEMO was found. This datum confirmed the diagnosis of NEMO deficiency.
The patient was followed by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) clinic in Bethesda, Maryland. She was given gamma interferon and all the listed antibiotics and was improving along with tapering his corticosteroid use.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 7-year history of refractory, multifocal granulomatous skin plaques, nodules, and ulcers across all four extremities and the trunk accompanied by recurrent high-grade fevers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Seven years prior to referral, the patient developed a painless, non-pruritic plaque on his right shoulder that spread to all four extremities; initially diagnosed as sarcoidosis and treated with corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine, repeat biopsies showed granulomas with numerous acid-fast bacilli, leading to a tentative diagnosis of leprosy and unsuccessful treatment with rifampin, clarithromycin, and minocycline. Attempts to taper corticosteroids triggered lesion exacerbation and fevers up to 105.0 F requiring hospitalization. After bone marrow biopsy grew Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI), he received 6 months of clarithromycin, ethambutol, rifampin, and prednisone 16 mg/day, but fevers persisted, new ulcerated and escharotic nodules erupted on the torso and limbs, and a repeat skin biopsy showing atypical dermal T-cells with positive TCR gene rearrangement prompted referral for suspected cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL).
subjective.past_medical_history: Childhood history of asthma and pneumonia, and adult recurrent sinusitis requiring sinus surgery. Family history was notable for a male cousin recently hospitalized with disseminated hepatic Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection. He denied international travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent high fevers (up to 105.0 F) and progressive disseminated skin plaques and ulcerated nodules; initial lesion was painless and non-pruritic.

objective.physical_examination: During prior progression, multiple ulcerations with overlying eschars on the right forearm and torso and large centrally ulcerated erythematous nodules on the right lower extremity were noted; at referral presentation, cutaneous examination revealed diffuse, well-circumscribed, raised erythematous scaly plaques measuring 3 to 4 inches in diameter without active ulceration.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematological workup during febrile hospitalization showed pancytopenia; HIV and HTLV-1/2 serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT revealed enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes. Initial bone marrow biopsy showed granulomas and AFB (culture-positive for MAI); repeat bone marrow core biopsy showed normocellular marrow with loosely formed granulomas of foamy histiocytes and a small clonal CD3+, CD4+, CD26+, CD7- T-cell population on flow cytometry. Repeat skin biopsies demonstrated superficial and deep dermal histiocytic infiltrates with scant small atypical lymphocytes (without epidermotropism) and numerous long beaded AFB; tissue cultures isolated clarithromycin/ethambutol/moxifloxacin-resistant MAI as well as Mycobacterium simiae. Targeted genetic sequencing of the IKK-gamma (NEMO) gene was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Sequencing identified a hemizygous splice-site mutation at the last base of exon 1b (`c.1-16G>C`) in the IKK-gamma (`IKBKG`/NEMO) gene causing abnormally spliced transcripts and reduced NEMO expression, confirming X-linked nuclear factor-kappa B essential modulator (NEMO) deficiency complicated by disseminated multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare and Mycobacterium simiae coinfection (ruling out leprosy, sarcoidosis, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma). Managed at the National Institutes of Health with subcutaneous interferon-gamma, tailored multidrug antimycobacterial therapy, and gradual corticosteroid tapering, the patient achieved steady clinical improvement.
